voiceover.text: Here's the squat from last time, held at the bottom. Bones can't move themselves, so something has to pull, and a muscle can only pull. Now try this. Hold a heavy bag with your elbow bent, then lower it slowly to your side. Which muscle is working? Most people say the triceps, because the elbow is straightening. But feel your arm, and it's the biceps that's hard. Why?

Of the three kinds of muscle, cardiac muscle works the heart, and smooth muscle lines vessels, airways and the gut, both without your control. Skeletal muscle is the kind you control. It attaches to bone through a tendon, and when it contracts, it pulls on the bone, and if it shortens, it draws the bone towards itself. It can't push the bone back. So muscles work in opposing pairs. The biceps pulls the forearm up, and only the triceps can pull it straight again, unless gravity does that job for free. Remember that, because it solves the bag.

Learn each major muscle with the action it produces, because a name alone answers nothing. At the shoulder, the deltoid abducts the arm. At the elbow, the biceps flexes and the triceps extends. In the trunk, the rectus abdominis flexes and the erector spinae extends. At the hip, the gluteus maximus extends. At the knee, the quadriceps on the front of the thigh extend it, and the hamstrings on the back flex it. The hamstrings also extend the hip, so they cross two joints. They're often strained in sprinting, because a sprint stride stretches them at both ends at once. At the ankle, the gastrocnemius and soleus plantar flex, and tibialis anterior dorsiflexes.

scenes.title: slow and fast twitch, and why the traits cluster

voiceover.text: Every muscle is a mix of fibres, the muscle cells, in two main types. Slow twitch fibres contract slowly with low force, but resist fatigue for hours. Fast twitch fibres contract quickly with high force, but tire within seconds to minutes. Now notice that the slow twitch traits all point the same way. These fibres work with oxygen, so they need capillaries to deliver it, mitochondria to use it, and myoglobin to store it. Fast twitch fibres work mainly without oxygen, so they need less of each.

Light effort recruits slow twitch fibres first, and fast twitch fibres join as the force needed rises. So a marathon runner relies on slow twitch fibres, and a sprinter or a weightlifter on fast twitch. The proportion in each person is largely inherited. Training doesn't turn slow fibres into fast ones, but it does improve the fibres you have.

Now, three ways a muscle can contract. In an isotonic concentric contraction, the muscle shortens under tension, because its force beats the resistance, like lifting a biceps curl. In an isotonic eccentric contraction, the muscle lengthens while still under tension, because the muscle lets the resistance win, slowly, while still pulling against it. It isn't switching off. It's braking, like lowering the curl, or lowering yourself into a chair. And in an isometric contraction, the muscle is tense but doesn't change length, so the joint doesn't move, like holding a plank.

That solves the bag. As you lower it, your elbow extends, but gravity is doing the extending for free. The biceps works eccentrically, braking the fall. So don't ask which muscle makes that joint action. Ask what is resisting the movement. When gravity makes the movement, the working muscle is the one on the other side, lengthening to control it. A muscle can brake a heavier load than it can lift, and eccentric work causes the most soreness a day or two later.

Because muscles only pull, they work in three roles. The agonist, or prime mover, contracts to produce the movement. The antagonist, on the opposite side of the joint, relaxes and lengthens to let it happen. And a stabiliser contracts, usually without moving, to hold a bone still, so the agonist has a firm base to pull from. These are roles, not muscles. Curling up, the biceps is the agonist and the triceps the antagonist. Pushing a weight away, they swap. But lowering a curl slowly doesn't swap them. The biceps is still the agonist, now working eccentrically.

Put both systems together in a squat. Going down, the hip and knee flex, and the quadriceps work eccentrically, braking against gravity. Coming up, the quadriceps are the agonist. They contract concentrically and pull on the tibia through the patellar tendon, so the knee extends. The gluteus maximus extends the hip, the hamstrings are the antagonist at the knee, though at the hip they help the gluteus maximus, and the trunk muscles hold still as stabilisers. And because the knee is a hinge, that pull can only produce extension. The muscles supply the force, and the skeleton decides what it can do.
Two things to remember. A muscle can only pull. And to find the working muscle, ask what is resisting the movement.

Two exam questions. First. A basketball player lands from a rebound, holds a crouched position for a moment, then jumps again. Identify the type of muscle contraction in the quadriceps during the landing, the hold and the jump. Pause here to answer.

Landing, the quadriceps lengthen under tension to absorb the force, so that's isotonic eccentric. Holding the crouch, they're tense but the knee angle doesn't change, so it's isometric. Jumping, they shorten to extend the knee, so it's isotonic concentric. The classic mistake is calling the landing concentric, just because the muscle is clearly working.
Second. Compare the characteristics and functions of slow twitch and fast twitch muscle fibres. Pause here to answer.

Put both fibre types in every sentence. Slow twitch fibres contract slowly with low force, whereas fast twitch fibres are fast and forceful. Slow twitch resist fatigue, whereas fast twitch tire quickly. Then explain the cluster: working with oxygen needs capillaries, mitochondria and myoglobin. Add a similarity and an event for each. The classic mistake is two separate paragraphs, which is two descriptions, not a comparison.

So, for any movement, name each muscle's role and its contraction type, and check what's resisting. Now look at the arm again. The forearm is a rigid bar, and the elbow is its pivot. That's a lever, and it obeys physics.
